patterns.name: Problem Classification
patterns.coreIdea: Classify a problem by its constraints, structure, required output, and operation model before selecting an algorithm. A correct classification sharply narrows the viable patterns and target complexity.

patterns.name: Complexity Analysis
patterns.coreIdea: Translate constraints into an allowable time and space budget, then reject algorithms that exceed it. Analyze total work, including preprocessing, queries, recursion, and amortized operations.

patterns.name: Invariant Design
patterns.coreIdea: Define a property that is true before and after every operation; that invariant becomes both the algorithm and its correctness argument. Track exactly which region or state is already valid.

patterns.name: State Design
patterns.coreIdea: Represent each partial solution with the smallest state that contains everything needed for the next decision. Good state design removes irrelevant history while preserving valid transitions.

patterns.name: Reduction
patterns.coreIdea: Transform an unfamiliar problem into a known pattern while preserving feasibility or optimality. The key is to prove that solutions correspond in both directions or that the transformed objective is equivalent.

patterns.name: Greedy Thinking
patterns.coreIdea: Choose the locally best action only when an exchange, dominance, or stay-ahead argument proves it cannot harm a global optimum. Greedy state usually retains the most flexible feasible partial solution.

patterns.name: Linear Scan
patterns.coreIdea: Traverse the sequence once while maintaining only the state needed for the processed prefix. Update the answer at each element without revisiting earlier positions.

patterns.name: Running Extremum and Kadane’s Algorithm
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain the best value ending at the current position and the best value seen globally. Discard a harmful prefix whenever restarting produces a better future candidate.

patterns.name: Frequency Counting
patterns.coreIdea: Replace repeated searching with a table from value to occurrence count. Frequency vectors also provide compact signatures for grouping, pairing, and equality tests.

patterns.name: In-Place Index Marking
keywords: Values lie in an index range
patterns.coreIdea: Use array positions as implicit storage, marking presence or state through signs, offsets, sentinels, or encoded values. Preserve enough of the original value to continue indexing correctly.

patterns.name: Cyclic Placement
keywords: Range 0 to n or 1 to n
patterns.coreIdea: Repeatedly swap each value into its designated index until every possible position is correct. Duplicates, missing values, and cycle structure then become visible from the remaining mismatches.

patterns.name: Prefix Sum
patterns.coreIdea: Store cumulative totals so any range aggregate becomes the difference of two prefixes. Pair prefix values with a hash map when the task asks how many earlier prefixes satisfy a target relation.

patterns.name: Prefix XOR
patterns.coreIdea: Store cumulative XOR so a range XOR is the XOR of two prefixes. For parity constraints, encode odd/even frequencies as a bitmask and match equal or nearby prefix states.

patterns.name: Prefix/Suffix Decomposition
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute summaries from the left and right so every index or split can be evaluated in constant time. The summaries may store sums, products, counts, extrema, or feasibility.

patterns.name: Difference Array
patterns.coreIdea: Record only how an update changes the boundary immediately before and after a range. One final prefix sum reconstructs every point’s accumulated value in linear time.

patterns.name: Coordinate Compression
patterns.coreIdea: Replace sparse values with dense ranks while preserving equality and order. This makes array-indexed data structures practical without changing comparison-based relationships.

patterns.name: Matrix Traversal and Direction Simulation
patterns.coreIdea: Model positions explicitly as row-column coordinates and centralize movement in direction vectors or shrinking boundaries. For transformations, reason by layers or coordinate mappings while preserving unprocessed cells.

patterns.name: Opposite-Direction Two Pointers
patterns.coreIdea: Place pointers at opposite ends and use order or symmetry to discard at least one endpoint after every comparison. The invariant guarantees that discarded candidates cannot improve the answer.

patterns.name: Same-Direction Two Pointers
patterns.coreIdea: Move both pointers forward, letting one scan new input while the other tracks a write position, match position, or valid boundary. Each element is processed only a constant number of times.

patterns.name: Fast-Slow Pointer
patterns.coreIdea: Advance two pointers at different speeds or with a fixed gap. Their meeting point, separation, or relative position reveals cycles, midpoints, and delayed targets without extra storage.

patterns.name: Expand Around Center
patterns.coreIdea: Treat every character and every gap as a possible center, then expand symmetrically while the endpoints match. This enumerates all palindromic substrings in quadratic time and constant auxiliary space.

patterns.name: Dutch National Flag / Three-Way Partitioning
keywords: Less than, equal to, greater than
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain disjoint regions for values below, equal to, and above a pivot while shrinking the unclassified region. Every swap preserves the region invariant and classifies at least one element.

patterns.name: Fixed Sliding Window
patterns.coreIdea: Build the first window, then slide it one position at a time by adding the entering element and removing the leaving element. This converts repeated range work into a linear scan.

patterns.name: Variable Sliding Window
keywords: At most or at least k
patterns.coreIdea: Expand the right boundary to gain elements and advance the left boundary whenever validity can be restored monotonically. Each boundary moves forward at most once per index, yielding linear time.

patterns.name: Monotonic Queue
keywords: DP over a bounded previous range
patterns.coreIdea: Keep candidate indices in a deque ordered by value and discard candidates that expire or can never be optimal. Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once.

patterns.name: Sort + Scan
patterns.coreIdea: Sort once so related values become adjacent or appear in a useful global order, then solve the transformed problem with a linear scan. The added ordering often replaces hashing or nested comparisons.

patterns.name: Sort + Greedy
patterns.coreIdea: Sort by the attribute that exposes a safe local choice, then commit greedily in that order. Correctness usually follows from exchanging the first differing choice with the greedy one.

patterns.name: Merge-Sort Counting
patterns.coreIdea: Divide by original index, count valid cross-half pairs while both halves are sorted, and merge them. Sorting inside the recursion reduces quadratic pair counting to logarithmic levels.

patterns.name: Quickselect / Partition Selection
patterns.coreIdea: Partition elements around a pivot and recurse only into the region containing the desired rank. Randomization gives expected linear time without fully sorting the input.

patterns.name: Sweep Line
patterns.coreIdea: Convert objects into ordered boundary events and sweep across one coordinate while maintaining the active set. Process equal-coordinate events with deliberate tie rules to preserve inclusivity and geometry.

patterns.name: Event Processing
patterns.coreIdea: Represent state changes as timestamped events and process them in a deterministic order, often with heaps for pending work and available resources. Jump directly to the next relevant time instead of simulating every time unit.

patterns.name: Classic Binary Search
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain a search interval known to contain any possible answer and discard half after each comparison. Choose one interval convention and update rules that guarantee progress and preserve the invariant.

patterns.name: Lower Bound
patterns.coreIdea: Find the first index whose value or predicate is at least the target or true. Maintain a half-open interval so the final boundary is also a valid insertion position when no equal value exists.

patterns.name: Upper Bound
patterns.coreIdea: Find the first position strictly greater than a target; the preceding position is the last value at most that target. Combining lower and upper bounds gives exact frequency and closed-range counts.

patterns.name: Binary Search on Answer
patterns.coreIdea: Turn optimization into a yes/no feasibility test whose truth changes once across the answer range. Binary-search that transition and return the first or last feasible value.

patterns.name: Parametric Search
patterns.coreIdea: Parameterize the objective by a candidate value and ask whether a problem-specific oracle can achieve it. Search the monotone parameter space, using exact boundaries for discrete values or controlled iterations for real values.

patterns.name: Stack Simulation and Cancellation
patterns.coreIdea: Store unresolved items on a stack; each new item either combines with, cancels, or is pushed after the current top.

patterns.name: Parentheses Matching
patterns.coreIdea: Track unmatched opening delimiters and validate each closing delimiter against the latest compatible opener. For one delimiter type, a balance counter may replace the stack.

patterns.name: Expression Evaluation
patterns.coreIdea: Separate values from operators and reduce operations when precedence or closing delimiters permit. Recursive descent is the equivalent choice when the grammar has nested structure.

patterns.name: Monotonic Increasing Stack
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain candidates in nondecreasing order, popping larger elements when a smaller value proves they can no longer be optimal or determines their boundary.

patterns.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack
patterns.coreIdea: Keep unresolved candidates in nonincreasing order; a larger incoming value resolves every smaller top and exposes its next-greater boundary.

patterns.name: Histogram and Maximal Rectangle
patterns.coreIdea: Treat each value as the limiting height of its maximal span, found with nearest-smaller boundaries. Convert each matrix row into a histogram when solving rectangular binary-grid variants.

patterns.name: Top K with a Heap
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain only the best k candidates in a heap whose root is the easiest retained item to evict. This reduces full sorting to roughly O(n log k).

patterns.name: Two Heaps
patterns.coreIdea: Split values across a max-heap for the lower partition and a min-heap for the upper partition, then rebalance sizes and boundary order after every update.

patterns.name: K-Way Merge
patterns.coreIdea: Place the current frontier of each sorted source in a heap, repeatedly extract the global next item, and advance only its source.

patterns.name: Heap Scheduling
patterns.coreIdea: Sort tasks by release time or deadline and use a heap to select the best currently feasible task, server, or resource at each decision point.

patterns.name: Heap with Lazy Deletion
patterns.coreIdea: Leave obsolete entries in the heap and record their invalidation separately. Discard stale roots only when they reach the top, preserving logarithmic updates.

patterns.name: Dummy Node
patterns.coreIdea: Attach a sentinel before the real head so insertions, deletions, and splices at the front use the same predecessor logic as internal nodes.

patterns.name: Linked-List Reversal
patterns.coreIdea: Walk the list while redirecting each next pointer toward the processed prefix, preserving the unprocessed suffix before every mutation.

patterns.name: Reverse in K-Groups
patterns.coreIdea: Locate a complete group, reverse exactly that node range, and reconnect its old head and new head to the neighboring segments without losing the suffix.

patterns.name: Linked-List Fast-Slow Pointer
patterns.coreIdea: Advance pointers at different speeds or with a fixed gap so their relative positions reveal a midpoint, suffix position, or repeated state in one pass.

patterns.name: Linked-List Merge
patterns.coreIdea: Compare the current nodes of sorted inputs, append the smaller candidate to a shared tail, and advance only its source.

patterns.name: Linked-List Cycle Detection
patterns.coreIdea: Move one pointer one step and another two steps; they meet exactly when a reachable cycle exists. Resetting one pointer to the start then reveals the cycle entry.

patterns.name: Divide-and-Conquer List Sorting
patterns.coreIdea: Split the list at its midpoint, recursively sort both halves, and merge them by relinking nodes. Bottom-up merging removes recursion-stack overhead.

patterns.name: Merge Intervals
patterns.coreIdea: Sort intervals by start, then extend the current merged interval while overlap continues and emit it when a gap begins.

patterns.name: Interval Scheduling
patterns.coreIdea: For unweighted selection, choosing the feasible interval with the earliest finish preserves the most future options. Weighted or capacity-limited variants add dynamic programming or a heap.

patterns.name: Interval Partitioning
patterns.coreIdea: Process intervals by start time and reuse the resource with the earliest finish whenever possible. Equivalently, the required resource count is the maximum number of concurrent intervals.

patterns.name: Exchange Argument
patterns.coreIdea: Show that replacing the first deviation from a greedy choice with the greedy choice cannot worsen an optimal solution. Repeating the exchange transforms some optimum into the greedy construction.

patterns.name: Greedy + Heap
patterns.coreIdea: Process candidates in a greedy order while a heap records chosen items, enabling the worst current choice to be replaced when feasibility or value improves.

patterns.name: Greedy Reachability and Coverage
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain the farthest boundary reachable with the decisions already committed, scanning all candidates available before that boundary to choose the next maximal extension.

patterns.name: Tree DFS
patterns.coreIdea: Define what a recursive call receives and returns for one subtree, then combine child results at the correct preorder, inorder, or postorder moment.

patterns.name: Tree BFS
patterns.coreIdea: Use a queue to process nodes in nondecreasing depth, usually freezing the current queue size to isolate one level at a time.

patterns.name: Binary Search Tree
patterns.coreIdea: Exploit the invariant that every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key is larger, enabling ordered search and sorted inorder traversal.

patterns.name: Divide-and-Conquer Tree Construction
patterns.coreIdea: Choose the root from the representation, partition the remaining data into left and right subproblems, and recursively construct both children.

patterns.name: Root-to-Leaf Path State
patterns.coreIdea: Carry the state accumulated from the root into each child and evaluate it at the relevant leaf or node. Restore mutable path state when recursion returns.

patterns.name: Tree DP
patterns.coreIdea: Define a compact state for each subtree and combine child states in postorder. When every node must become the root of an answer, propagate complementary information with rerooting.

patterns.name: Tree Diameter
patterns.coreIdea: At each node, combine its two best downward paths to form a path through that node while returning only the best single downward path to its parent.

patterns.name: Lowest Common Ancestor
patterns.coreIdea: For one query, return the first node whose subtrees collectively contain both targets. For many queries, preprocess jump pointers or an Euler representation to answer ancestors efficiently.

patterns.name: Tree Serialization
patterns.coreIdea: Encode both values and structural boundaries in a deterministic traversal so decoding can reconstruct the same tree. Canonical encodings also turn structural equality into signature equality.

patterns.name: Morris Traversal
patterns.coreIdea: Temporarily thread each node's inorder predecessor back to the node, using the second encounter to distinguish completed left subtrees. Remove every thread to restore the original tree.

patterns.name: Graph Modeling and Adjacency Representation
patterns.coreIdea: Translate entities into vertices and relationships into edges, preserving direction, weight, and multiplicity. Choose an adjacency list, matrix, edge list, or implicit neighbor generator to match the graph’s density and operations.

patterns.name: Graph DFS
patterns.coreIdea: Explore one path completely before backtracking, marking each vertex when first entered. DFS naturally exposes components, ancestry, cycles, and postorder dependencies.

patterns.name: Graph BFS
patterns.coreIdea: Explore vertices in nondecreasing distance from the source using a queue. The first visit to a state gives its shortest path when every transition has equal cost.

patterns.name: Multi-Source BFS
patterns.coreIdea: Insert every source into the queue at distance zero, then run one BFS wave. This computes each state’s distance to its nearest source and correctly simulates simultaneous propagation.

patterns.name: State-Space BFS
patterns.coreIdea: Treat each complete configuration—not merely its position—as a vertex, then BFS across legal transitions. Include every history-dependent feature needed to determine future moves in the visited key.

patterns.name: Topological Sort
patterns.coreIdea: Order a directed graph so every prerequisite appears before its dependents. Failure to process all vertices proves that a directed cycle prevents a valid ordering.

patterns.name: Union Find / Disjoint Set Union
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain a partition of elements under repeated unions and connectivity queries. Path compression and union by size or rank make the amortized operation cost effectively constant.

patterns.name: Bipartite Coloring
patterns.coreIdea: Assign opposite colors across every edge using DFS or BFS; a same-color edge proves an odd cycle and makes the partition impossible. A valid bipartition also unlocks matching and minimum-vertex-cover reductions.

patterns.name: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
patterns.coreIdea: Repeatedly finalize the unsettled state with the smallest known distance and relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative transition costs guarantee that a finalized distance cannot later improve.

patterns.name: 0–1 BFS
keywords: Edge weights are zero or one
patterns.coreIdea: Run Dijkstra’s greedy relaxation with a deque: push zero-cost transitions to the front and one-cost transitions to the back. This preserves nondecreasing distances in linear time.

patterns.name: Bellman–Ford
patterns.coreIdea: Relax every edge repeatedly so shortest paths using progressively more edges become available. A further improvement after the required rounds reveals a reachable negative cycle.

patterns.name: Floyd–Warshall
patterns.coreIdea: Allow vertices as intermediates one by one, updating every pair through the newly permitted vertex. The same recurrence computes shortest paths, reachability closure, or other path-composable relations.

patterns.name: Minimum Spanning Tree
keywords: Minimax path in an undirected graph
patterns.coreIdea: Select the cheapest edges that connect every vertex without creating unnecessary cycles. Cut and cycle properties justify both Kruskal’s global edge ordering and Prim’s expanding frontier.

patterns.name: Subsets Backtracking
patterns.coreIdea: At each candidate, branch on whether to include it and backtrack after exploring that choice. Sorting and same-depth duplicate skipping produce unique subsets without global deduplication.

patterns.name: Permutations Backtracking
patterns.coreIdea: Build an ordering one position at a time, choosing among unused candidates and undoing each choice on return. Frequency maps or same-depth duplicate skipping avoid repeated permutations.

patterns.name: Combinations Backtracking
patterns.coreIdea: Extend a partial combination only with candidates at or after a controlled start index. Moving or retaining that index distinguishes single-use choices from reusable choices and prevents reordered duplicates.

patterns.name: Constraint Search
patterns.coreIdea: Assign one decision at a time and immediately reject partial states that violate a constraint or cannot beat the current best. Strong variable ordering, candidate ordering, and bounds determine practical performance.

patterns.name: Grid Path Backtracking
patterns.coreIdea: Explore each legal neighboring cell, mark it for the current path, and unmark it when backtracking. Prune as soon as the path cannot satisfy the remaining target or improve the best result.

patterns.name: Fibonacci DP
patterns.coreIdea: Express the current answer from a constant number of immediately preceding states. Once the base cases are correct, a left-to-right recurrence can usually be compressed to constant space.

patterns.name: Linear DP
patterns.coreIdea: Define a state for the optimal result on a prefix or ending at an index, then transition from earlier valid states. Iterate in dependency order and compress memory when only a bounded history is needed.

patterns.name: Grid DP
patterns.coreIdea: Treat each cell as a state whose dependencies are neighboring cells reached earlier in a valid traversal order. Expand the state when direction, resource, or multiple-agent information affects future moves.

patterns.name: 0/1 Knapsack
keywords: Use each item at most once
patterns.coreIdea: For every item, choose between excluding it and consuming capacity once to include it. Iterate capacities backward in one-dimensional implementations so the same item cannot be reused.

patterns.name: Unbounded Knapsack
patterns.coreIdea: Allow a choice to transition from a state updated during the same item’s iteration, enabling repeated use. Loop order determines whether the DP counts combinations, permutations, or merely optimizes value.

patterns.name: Coin Change
patterns.coreIdea: Define the amount as capacity and choose a recurrence matching the question: minimum coins, unordered combinations, ordered sequences, or bounded counts. The item/amount loop order is part of the state semantics.

patterns.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
patterns.coreIdea: Track the smallest possible tail for an increasing subsequence of each length, replacing tails by lower bound. Use quadratic DP when counts, reconstruction, or richer compatibility transitions are required.

patterns.name: Longest Common Subsequence
patterns.coreIdea: For each pair of prefixes, either match equal final elements or skip one final element and keep the better result. The same alignment table supports reconstruction and many insertion/deletion reductions.

patterns.name: Edit Distance
patterns.coreIdea: Define a state for transforming one prefix into another and transition by matching, inserting, deleting, or replacing the final symbol. Add dimensions when edits have budgets, modes, or compressed effects.

patterns.name: Interval DP
keywords: Choose the first or last operation
patterns.coreIdea: Define the answer for every interval and transition by choosing a boundary action or split point. Process intervals from shorter to longer so all subinterval dependencies are already solved.

patterns.name: Partition DP
patterns.coreIdea: Let a state cover a prefix with a fixed number of completed groups, and enumerate the previous cut. Precompute segment costs and optimize the cut transition when monotonicity or convexity permits.

patterns.name: State Machine DP
patterns.coreIdea: Represent each prefix by a small finite set of modes and update every mode through legal transitions. The state machine makes mutually exclusive histories explicit while keeping the state space constant per position.

patterns.name: Digit DP
patterns.coreIdea: Build numbers digit by digit while tracking whether the current prefix is tight to the bound, has started, and satisfies the required aggregate state. Compute a range answer as the difference between two prefix counts.

patterns.name: Bitmask DP
patterns.coreIdea: Encode the chosen or completed subset as an integer mask, then transition by adding, removing, or partitioning bits. This turns history-dependent subset choices into a finite state graph of size roughly 2ⁿ.

patterns.name: Probability DP
patterns.coreIdea: Store the probability or count distribution for each state and push mass through every random transition. Carefully define terminal states, normalization, and whether the recurrence computes probability, expectation, or favorable counts.

patterns.name: Game DP
patterns.coreIdea: Define each state from the current player’s perspective and assume the opponent responds optimally. Boolean games use winning/losing transitions, while score games often maximize the current score difference.

patterns.name: DAG DP
patterns.coreIdea: Process states in topological order, or memoize DFS on an acyclic dependency graph, so every transition reads finalized predecessors. DAG DP generalizes sequence and grid DP to arbitrary partial orders.

patterns.name: Trie
patterns.coreIdea: Store strings as paths through shared prefix nodes so insertion and lookup depend on key length rather than dictionary size. Binary tries apply the same idea to bits for XOR optimization.

patterns.name: Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP)
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute failure links from the pattern so a mismatch reuses the longest compatible prefix instead of restarting. This gives linear preprocessing and linear scanning.

patterns.name: Z Algorithm
patterns.coreIdea: The Z-array records the longest prefix match beginning at every position. A maintained matching interval lets all values be computed in linear time.

patterns.name: Rabin–Karp
patterns.coreIdea: Hash the pattern and update the text window’s hash in constant time as it slides. Verify hash matches or use multiple hashes when collisions cannot be tolerated.

patterns.name: Rolling Hash
patterns.coreIdea: Represent substrings with prefix-based fingerprints so equal-length substring hashes are extracted in constant time. Use normalized powers, two moduli, or direct verification to control collisions.

patterns.name: Manacher’s Algorithm
patterns.coreIdea: Reuse the mirror radius inside the rightmost known palindrome, expanding only beyond its boundary. A separator transformation can unify odd- and even-length palindromes.

patterns.name: Aho–Corasick
patterns.coreIdea: Build a trie of all patterns and add failure links that preserve the longest suffix which is also a trie prefix. The resulting automaton reports all dictionary matches in one pass over the text.

patterns.name: Suffix Array
patterns.coreIdea: Sort all suffixes by lexicographic rank and pair the order with an LCP array. Substring searches and repeated-substring questions then become range or neighbor operations on suffix ranks.

patterns.name: Suffix Automaton
patterns.coreIdea: Build the minimal automaton recognizing every substring by extending one character at a time and cloning states when needed. State lengths and suffix links compactly encode substring occurrence classes.

patterns.name: Bitwise XOR
patterns.coreIdea: Use XOR’s cancellation, commutativity, and bitwise independence to remove paired contributions or encode parity. For optimization, choose opposite bits greedily through a binary trie or basis.

patterns.name: Bitmask Enumeration
patterns.coreIdea: Encode membership of a small set in the bits of an integer and enumerate masks from zero to (2^n-1). Bit tests, insertion, removal, and compatibility checks then become constant-time operations.

patterns.name: Submask Enumeration
keywords: Assign one group at a time
patterns.coreIdea: Enumerate every submask of a mask with `sub = (sub - 1) & mask`, touching exactly the valid subsets. This is the standard transition engine for partitioning and group-assignment DP over small sets.

patterns.name: Binary Lifting
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute the result of (2^j) jumps from every state, then decompose each requested jump count into set bits. The same doubling table supports ancestors, functional graphs, and path aggregates.

patterns.name: Fenwick Tree
patterns.coreIdea: Store partial prefix aggregates in ranges determined by the least significant set bit. Point updates and prefix queries both take logarithmic time with a compact array representation.
commonAlgorithms: Range update with dual Fenwick trees

patterns.name: Segment Tree
patterns.coreIdea: Recursively partition an index range and store an aggregate for each segment. Any query interval decomposes into logarithmically many canonical nodes, while point updates repair one root-to-leaf path.

patterns.name: Lazy Segment Tree
patterns.coreIdea: Attach pending update tags to segment-tree nodes and push them to children only when required. Entire covered ranges can then be updated and queried in logarithmic time.

patterns.name: Sparse Table
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute answers for every power-of-two interval. Idempotent range queries such as minimum, maximum, GCD, AND, or OR can then combine two overlapping blocks in constant time.

patterns.name: Ordered Set
patterns.coreIdea: Maintain keys in sorted order while supporting logarithmic insertion, deletion, and neighbor queries. Add counts or augmented subtree sizes when duplicates or rank selection matter.

patterns.name: Strongly Connected Components
patterns.coreIdea: Partition a directed graph into maximal groups whose vertices can all reach one another. Contracting each group produces a DAG on which dependency and reachability reasoning becomes simpler.

patterns.name: Bridges
patterns.coreIdea: During DFS, compare each child’s low-link value with its parent’s discovery time. A tree edge is a bridge exactly when the child’s subtree cannot reach the parent or an ancestor without that edge.

patterns.name: Articulation Points
patterns.coreIdea: Track discovery and low-link times in an undirected DFS tree. A non-root vertex is an articulation point when a child subtree has no back edge above it; the root is critical when it has multiple DFS children.

patterns.name: Euler Tour
patterns.coreIdea: Record each node’s DFS entry and exit positions so every subtree becomes a contiguous interval. Tree queries can then be reduced to array range queries or timestamp comparisons.

patterns.name: Euler Path and Circuit
patterns.coreIdea: Check degree and connectivity conditions, then consume edges with Hierholzer’s algorithm and append vertices during backtracking. Reversing that postorder yields an Euler trail using every edge once.

patterns.name: Maximum Flow
patterns.coreIdea: Send flow from a source to a sink while maintaining residual capacities that allow earlier choices to be reversed. Many allocation and matching constraints become capacities in a flow network.

patterns.name: Minimum Cut
patterns.coreIdea: After computing maximum flow, vertices reachable from the source in the residual graph define a minimum source–sink cut. Node splitting converts vertex-removal costs into edge capacities.

patterns.name: Bipartite Matching
keywords: Assign left side to right side
patterns.coreIdea: Model candidates and resources as opposite partitions and add edges for valid pairings. Augmenting paths repeatedly reroute existing matches to increase the matching size.

patterns.name: Greatest Common Divisor
patterns.coreIdea: Use Euclid’s algorithm to replace ((a,b)) with ((b,a \bmod b)) until the remainder is zero. GCD normalizes ratios, exposes periodic structure, and combines with LCM for divisibility counting.

patterns.name: Modular Arithmetic
patterns.coreIdea: Replace integers by congruent remainder classes while preserving addition and multiplication. Normalize negative values and postpone division until a valid modular inverse is available.

patterns.name: Fast Power
patterns.coreIdea: Decompose the exponent into binary powers and repeatedly square the base. This reduces exponentiation from linear to logarithmic multiplications and generalizes to matrices and other monoids.

patterns.name: Modular Inverse
patterns.coreIdea: Replace division by multiplication with an inverse satisfying (a a^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod m). Compute inverses with extended Euclid when coprime or Fermat’s theorem under a prime modulus.

patterns.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
patterns.coreIdea: Mark multiples of each discovered prime, starting from its square, to preprocess primality for an entire range. A smallest-prime-factor sieve also makes repeated factorization efficient.

patterns.name: Prime Factorization
patterns.coreIdea: Express every positive integer as a product of prime powers and reason independently about their exponents. Trial division is sufficient for one small number; smallest-prime-factor preprocessing handles many values.

patterns.name: Matrix Exponentiation
patterns.coreIdea: Encode a fixed-order linear recurrence as multiplication by a transition matrix, then raise that matrix to a large power. Binary exponentiation reduces the number of transitions from linear to logarithmic.

patterns.name: Combinatorics
patterns.coreIdea: Count outcomes structurally with permutations, combinations, multinomials, inclusion–exclusion, or constructive recurrences. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials when many modular binomial queries are required.

patterns.name: Catalan Numbers
patterns.coreIdea: Catalan objects split around a distinguished root into independent left and right objects, yielding (C_n=\sum C_iC_{n-1-i}). Use the recurrence for structural DP or the closed form for pure counting.
